newsitem.title: USA: RU 486 pill could transform U.S. abortion debate.
newsitem.headline: RU 486 pill could transform U.S. abortion debate.

text.p: A chemical compound discovered in a French laboratory more than a decade ago could transform the abortion debate in America, an issue so explosive and sensitive that it has caused fissures in American politics and murders at American clinics.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday deemed "approvable" mifepristone, better known as RU 486, the French abortion drug.

That means the FDA believes it is safe and effective, but the non-profit Population Council must provide the FDA some more information on labeling and manufacturing, conditions that the Population Council said it expects to fulfill.

However, some abortion rights activists have concerns about whether all the obstacles -- technical and especially financial -- can be overcome to get the drug swiftly to market given all the political overtones of the abortion debate.

"There's no manufacturer standing ready and able to make it available for American women next week, next month, or even, I believe, next year," said Janet Benshoof, president of the Center for Reproductive Law and Policy. "If you've just found out you're pregnant -- start picking names."

Yet both sides in the abortion debate that has raged in the courts, in state legislatures, in national political campaigns and in the clinics regard FDA approval as a watershed that will make it easier for women to get an abortion early in pregnancy.
The 1973 Roe vs. Wade Supreme Court ruling protecting abortion rights has stood repeated legal challenges. But although abortion is legal throughout the United States, access is very uneven.
In most big cities, abortion is available, although some states have imposed waiting periods or restrictions on minors.
But in more than four out of five U.S. counties, no doctors perform abortions. Many medical students, including future obstetricians, do not learn how to do them.
Clinics have been vandalized and bombed. Patients have been accosted and harassed. Doctors and clinic workers have been murdered.

But a pill means a woman does not have to go to a clinic. Early in her pregnancy -- the Population Council is seeking approval for the drug through the seventh week -- she just has to go to the doctor's office and swallow some pills that will block a hormone essential to pregnancy.

It is by no means as simple as taking an aspirin. The patient requires close medical supervision and may experience discomfort. In most cases she will require a return visit to the doctor's office a few days later to take a second drug to start contractions to expel the embryo.
But no protesters lingering outside with posters and pamphlets can tell who is getting an abortion, and who is just going in to her doctor for a stomach ache or sore throat.

"I believe it will help reduce clinic violence," said Eleanor Smeal, president of the Feminist Majority. "And we already know that many more doctors will be willing to administer mifepristone than do surgical abortions."

Anti-abortion rights groups have fought hard against the drug, accusing President Bill Clinton and FDA commissioner David Kessler of politicizing the drug approval process to advance an abortion agenda.

The Clinton administration helped negotiate the unusual arrangement in which a non-profit group, instead of the pharmaceutical maker, sponsored the drug before the FDA and coordinated the clinical trials.
"For us it doesn't really change anything -- National Right to Life Committee works by educating people about abortion," said the anti-abortion group's spokeswoman Michele Arocha Allen.

"We are seeing yet another way to kill unborn children, this time by using their mothers as guinea pigs as well," she said, arguing that long-term effects of the drug have not been adequately studied.
Other anti-abortion groups were more blunt.
"Pro-life activists around the world consider RU 486 to be the modern day equivalent to the Zyklon-B gas used by Hitler," Operation Rescue said in a statement.
